messages.content: You are a careful analyst. Answer strictly and only from the documents provided in the user message. After every factual claim, cite the supporting document id in square brackets, like [doc-2]. If a fact needed for the answer is absent from the documents, say "not in the documents" for that part. Do not use outside knowledge and do not invent figures.

Here are three documents about the relocation of the Harwick Maritime Museum collection. Read them carefully and answer the question at the end.

[doc-1] Harwick Maritime Museum: Collection Inventory and Condition Survey (March 2026)

The survey was carried out between 5 January and 20 March 2026 by twelve museum staff and four contract conservators as the evidence base for the museum's relocation from the Harwick Quay building. The collection comprises 48,200 accessioned items: 31,400 archival items (charts, logbooks, crew agreements, photographic negatives and ship plans), 9,700 three-dimensional objects, 5,850 textiles including 310 flags and 92 sails, 212 paintings, and 1,038 items in other categories such as scientific instruments and ship's fittings. The oversized cohort numbers 640 items exceeding two metres in any dimension, among them 74 large ship models in glazed cases, 18 carved figureheads, the 9.6-metre steam launch Wren, and a triple-expansion marine engine weighing 11.2 tonnes.

Condition grading followed the museum's four-band scale: 41% of items graded A (stable, fit to travel), 37% graded B (minor treatment desirable), 17% graded C (treatment required), and 5% graded D (unfit to travel without intervention). From bands C and D, 1,940 objects are flagged for stabilization before transport - principally consolidation of flaking paint on ship models, humidification and flattening of distorted vellum charts, and mount-making for fragile rigging. The paintings store adds 12 canvases that need facing before any movement.

Integrated pest management checks found live webbing clothes moth in the textile store and evidence of active woodborer in two model cases. In total 345 items - 260 textiles and 85 organic or taxidermy objects - are declared a quarantine cohort: museum policy requires every item in this cohort to complete anoxic treatment before it may enter the new building, without exception. The affected sail collection includes the museum's largest single textile, the 68-square-metre mainsail of the ketch Speranza.

Hazardous materials were identified on 380 items: lead-based paint on 214 objects, 61 mercury barometers and artificial horizons, 17 radium-dial instruments, and asbestos gaskets and lagging in the engine components. These require sealed handling, separate manifests, and, for the radium dials, a licensed carrier. The survey also retagged 46,900 items with new barcodes; reconciliation against the 2019 register surfaced 1,300 discrepancies, of which 210 remained unresolved when the survey closed - mostly location mismatches in the archive basement, plus 41 items not found at their registered locations.

Valuations were refreshed for insurance purposes. Twenty-two objects are individually valued above 1.0 million pounds, with a combined value of 41 million; the two highest are the Turner-attributed oil "Storm off Harwick Ness" at 8.4 million and the 1698 Board of Ordnance chart atlas at 3.1 million. A further 190 objects sit between 250,000 and 1.0 million pounds. The survey recommends that the 22 top objects be condition-checked jointly with the insurer's representative immediately before movement.

The report concludes with three priorities for the move planners: complete stabilization of the 1,940-object cohort in time to feed the packing schedule; begin the anoxic quarantine program early enough that treated items, not untreated ones, form the head of the object-move queue; and resolve the 210 outstanding register discrepancies, since an unreconciled register was the root cause of the two losses recorded during the museum's 1987 store consolidation.

[doc-2] Harwick Quay to Meridian Wharf: Relocation Logistics and Transport Plan (April 2026)

Ashfield Fine Art Logistics was appointed principal contractor on 2 April 2026 under a fixed-price contract of 4.1 million pounds. The approved route from Harwick Quay to the Meridian Wharf Collection Centre runs 14.3 kilometres with two diversions around low bridges; movements wider than 4.2 metres require police escort and are scheduled between 01:00 and 05:00. The fleet assigns five climate-controlled air-ride vehicles held at 18-22 degrees Celsius and 45-55% relative humidity, with shock and tilt loggers fitted to every crate graded B or below and to all paintings.

The move is phased. Phase 1 (4 May to 26 June 2026) transfers the 31,400 archival items in 1,900 standard archive containers over 96 vehicle runs, feeding the new archive store directly. Phase 2 (6 July to 25 September 2026) moves the three-dimensional objects, textiles and paintings: an estimated 320 vehicle runs carrying 8,400 custom crates plus soft-packed material, at a sustained tempo of no more than six runs per day across the twelve-week window. Phase 3 (5 to 30 October 2026) handles the 640 oversized items as 52 special movements, including crane lifts for the figureheads, a low-loader for the steam launch Wren, and a night closure of Meridian Bridge for the 11.2-tonne engine.

Two scheduling rules govern Phase 2. First, no object flagged for stabilization or quarantine may be scheduled until conservation signs it off; the plan therefore reserves the first three weeks of Phase 2 exclusively for material that has already cleared treatment. Second, the packing tempo is bounded by the crate shop, which peaks at 160 crates per week with 28 technicians in seven teams; crates for the pest-treatment cohort must additionally be gas-tight so that anoxia holds between chamber and vehicle.

High-value objects follow a separate protocol. Each of the 22 objects valued above one million pounds travels as the sole high-value item on its vehicle, accompanied by two escorts, with no two high-value objects on the road on the same day. Every such movement requires 72-hour advance notification to the insurer, a fresh condition report signed at both ends, and GPS tracking shared with the museum's security room. The plan schedules these 22 movements as a distinct strand, provisionally in weeks 3 through 11 of Phase 2 with the overflow into Phase 3.

On budget, crating accounts for 1.32 million pounds, transport 0.86 million, specialist staffing 1.04 million, storage furniture and equipment at the receiving end 0.54 million, and contingency 0.34 million. The contingency assumes up to eight weather-lost days and one vehicle substitution. Key risks logged in the plan are: late completion of conservation stabilization compressing the head of Phase 2; the quarantine chamber throughput at Meridian Wharf, which the contractor does not control; harbour festival road closures on 18-20 July; and any insurer refusal of a scheduled high-value movement, which cannot be absorbed without extending Phase 2. The plan states as an explicit assumption that all insurance endorsements required for the high-value strand will be in place before 1 July 2026, and it assigns responsibility for obtaining them to the museum registrar, not to the contractor.

[doc-3] Meridian Wharf Collection Centre: Readiness and Insurance Assessment (May 2026)

The assessment, commissioned by the museum's trustees from Calder Heritage Consulting, covers building readiness, environmental performance, quarantine capacity and insurance arrangements as of 15 May 2026.

The Meridian Wharf Collection Centre offers 11,800 square metres of storage across four climate zones: the archive store at 18 degrees Celsius and 40% relative humidity, the general object store at 19 degrees and 50%, a metals store held at 35% relative humidity, and a combined paintings and textiles store at 21 degrees and 52%. Commissioning trials between 10 February and 28 April 2026 held relative humidity within 2.8 percentage points and temperature within 0.9 degrees over a 30-day soak test in each zone. Fire protection uses a hypoxic-air system maintaining 15.1% oxygen in the archive store and pre-action sprinklers elsewhere. Racking provides 14.6 linear kilometres of archival shelving, 3,900 pallet positions, and an oversize hall with a 20-tonne gantry crane.

The quarantine suite contains two anoxia chambers of 30 cubic metres each, operating 21-day cycles at 0.1% oxygen and 50% relative humidity. Realistic combined throughput is about 120 crated textile or organic items per cycle, though large single items reduce this sharply: the assessor calculates that the Speranza mainsail will occupy one chamber for a full cycle on its own. Given the size of the museum's declared quarantine cohort, the assessor concludes the program needs at least three back-to-back cycles and recommends that the first chamber loads begin no later than the first week of May 2026 if treated material is to be available when object moves begin; at the assessment date the chambers had not yet run a live load, only the commissioning cycle.

Insurance is placed with a Lloyd's syndicate through Marchbanks Specie. The collection is insured for a total of 212 million pounds at the new site once intruder-alarm commissioning completes, expected on 20 June 2026. Transit cover is subject to two limits: an any-one-vehicle limit of 9.5 million pounds and an any-one-day aggregate of 15 million pounds for museum property on the road. Objects individually valued above 5 million pounds require a named-item endorsement and carriage by the insurer's approved specialist courier rather than by the principal contractor; as of the assessment date, named-item endorsements had been issued for two objects only - the Turner-attributed painting and the 1698 chart atlas - and the approved-courier arrangement for the painting was still in negotiation. The syndicate has additionally made acceptance of the transit schedule conditional on the museum closing the register discrepancies identified in the pre-move survey, citing the audit requirement in clause 14.2 of the policy.

Security and receiving arrangements otherwise pass: the loading dock provides an enclosed, alarmed airlock able to hold two vehicles; staff inductions for 31 Ashfield personnel completed on 9 May; and the dock's environmental curtain, specified to keep the dock within 5 percentage points of the stores' relative humidity during unloading, is the single outstanding fit-out item, with installation promised by 30 June 2026. The assessor's overall verdict is that the building is ready for Phase 1 archives and conditionally ready for Phase 2, the conditions being the quarantine program start, the insurance endorsements, and the register reconciliation.

Question: Drawing on all three documents, determine whether Phase 2 can begin on 6 July 2026 as planned and remain compliant. Specifically: (1) reconcile the size of the quarantine cohort in [doc-1] with the anoxia chamber throughput, cycle length and recommended start date in [doc-3] and with the Phase 2 rule in [doc-2] that reserves the first three weeks for treated material - is the treatment timeline arithmetically feasible, and what is the latest viable date for the first chamber load? (2) check the high-value movement strand in [doc-2] against the transit insurance limits and endorsement status in [doc-3] and the valuations in [doc-1], and state which, if any, of the 22 high-value objects cannot currently travel under the policy and why; (3) list every precondition that one document imposes and another document shows as unmet as of mid-May 2026. Cite a document id in square brackets for every figure you use, and where the documents do not contain a needed fact, say explicitly that it is not in the documents.
